title: Understanding Levels & Compensation Bands
summary: The level a company assigns you sets a comp band, a raise trajectory, and a scope expectation for years — which is why it matters more than any single negotiated number, and why it gets locked in before you ever see an offer letter.

slides.markdown:
Every offer sits inside a **level** — an internal rung (Associate, SDE II, L4, T4, whatever the company's ladder calls it) that determines your **comp band**: the min/max range for base, the bonus target percentage, and the equity grant range the company is allowed to offer. The level is usually locked in during the interview loop, well before you see a number.

This matters because the band, not your specific negotiated point inside it, is what compounds. Two candidates who both negotiate hard for +5% will end up far apart five years later if one of them is a level lower, because every future raise, refresher grant, and promotion case is calculated as a percentage of the lower band.

This topic covers how bands actually work, how to read your own level against the market, and why fighting for a level is usually a better trade than fighting for a number inside the wrong level.

A **level** is the company's internal answer to "how much scope, ambiguity, and impact do we expect from this person, and how much are we willing to pay for it." It's assigned by the hiring committee (or the hiring manager plus a leveling review) based on your interview performance and your résumé's demonstrated scope — not by you, and not by a recruiter alone.

Critically, the level is usually **fixed before the comp conversation starts**. The recruiter can flex your base or equity within the band tied to your level; they almost never have authority to move you into a different level's band without a re-review, because that review touches headcount planning, internal pay equity, and the leveling committee's calibration — not just your own offer.

That's why the highest-leverage negotiation often isn't "can I get $15k more," it's "can this be leveled as a senior rather than a mid-level" — asked as early as possible, ideally before an offer is even drafted.

slides.sectionTitle: How a comp band is structured
slides.subTitle: Base, bonus target, equity range
slides.markdown:
A band is really three separate ranges stacked together, each with its own flexibility:

| Component | What it means | How much it flexes |
|---|---|---|
| Base salary | Fixed cash, paid biweekly/monthly | Usually a $10-25k range within a level, least negotiable at the very top |
| Bonus target | % of base, paid annually, tied to company + individual performance | Sometimes negotiable as a guaranteed first-year floor |
| Equity grant | RSUs or options, vesting over 3-4 years | Often the most flexible lever, since it's a one-time grant decision, not a recurring cost |

Recruiters usually have real discretion over the **top of the base range** and the **equity grant size**, because both are one-time or slow-moving decisions. They have far less discretion over bonus target percentages, since those are usually set at the company or org level and applied uniformly.

Knowing which lever is actually flexible changes what you push on: asking for a 2% bump to a fixed bonus target wastes a negotiation round that could have gone toward equity.

slides.subTitle: A rough equivalence table
slides.markdown:
Level names don't map 1:1 across companies, but a rough equivalence for individual-contributor software roles looks like this:

| Rough band | Example titles | Typical years of experience |
|---|---|---|
| Entry | New Grad, L3, SDE I, E3 | 0-2 |
| Mid | L4, SDE II, E4, T4 | 2-5 |
| Senior | L5, Senior SDE, E5, T5 | 5-8 |
| Staff | L6, Principal SDE, E6, T6 | 8-12+ |
| Senior Staff / Principal | L7+, E7+ | 12+ |

Treat this as a starting orientation, not gospel — some companies compress two of these into one level, and a "Senior" title at a small startup can map to anywhere from mid to staff depending on how inflated the company's titles run. The safest anchor is **scope**, not title: what decisions were you trusted to make alone, how large was the system or team you influenced, and could you defend that scope in a leveling conversation.

slides.sectionTitle: Where to find real leveling and comp data
slides.markdown:
Before any negotiation, gather three kinds of data:

- **Crowdsourced comp data** (levels.fyi, Blind, Glassdoor's salary tool) for the specific company, level, and location you're targeting — not a national average, which hides huge city and level variance.
- **Your own network** — a two-minute message to a former colleague who works there now is worth more than any aggregator, because they can tell you what the *current* band actually is, not last year's.
- **The recruiter directly** — asking "what's the band for this level at this location" is a completely normal question; a recruiter who refuses to give any range at all before your first offer is a mild yellow flag, not a hard stop.

Cross-reference at least two sources before you form a target number. A single levels.fyi data point can be stale, self-reported inaccurately, or from a different location's cost-of-living adjustment, and anchoring hard on one bad number wastes credibility in the actual negotiation.

slides.sectionTitle: A higher number at a low level vs. a level-up at a lower number
slides.subTitle: Compare
slides.markdown:
A common trap: comparing two offers purely on first-year total comp when they land at different levels.

| | Offer A: Mid-level, aggressive number | Offer B: Senior level, standard number |
|---|---|---|
| Year 1 total comp | Higher (recruiter stretched the mid-level band) | Slightly lower (standard senior-band number) |
| Base salary ceiling | Capped at mid-level band max | Capped at senior-level band max (meaningfully higher) |
| Next promotion | Mid -> Senior, a real promo case required | Senior -> Staff, but you're already inside the senior band |
| 3-year trajectory | Bounded by mid-level raises until promoted | Compounds off a higher base from day one |

Offer A can look better on a single spreadsheet row and still be the worse long-term trade, because every future raise percentage applies to a lower starting base, and a promotion isn't guaranteed on any particular timeline. The level is the compounding variable; the year-one number is not.

slides.sectionTitle: Accepting a lowballed level just to get in the door
slides.subTitle: Pitfall
slides.markdown:
A common piece of bad advice: "take the lower level, you can always get promoted fast once you're in." In practice, promotion cycles are slower and more political than onboarding optimism assumes — most companies require 12-24 months of demonstrated scope at your *current* level before even considering a promotion packet, and the packet itself competes against a limited budget of promotions per cycle.

Meanwhile, your starting level anchors your manager's expectations of you from day one. A manager who onboarded you as mid-level tends to keep assigning mid-level-scoped work, which then makes it harder to build the very promotion case you need, since you're rarely handed staff-scoped problems as a mid-level engineer.

If you have real leverage — a competing offer, a strong internal referral, clear evidence of scope from your résumé — push on level *before* accepting, not after. "I'll take it and prove myself" is a much weaker position than "here's why this should be leveled a step higher," asked while the company still wants to close you.

slides.sectionTitle: A worked example: pushing on level before the offer
slides.subTitle: Concrete example
slides.markdown:
```
Situation: Recruiter calls to say the team wants to move forward, level TBD
pending final calibration, likely mid-level (L4).

Candidate's response (before any number is discussed):
"I'm glad it went well. Before we get to comp — I led the migration of a
payments service end-to-end at my last job, owned the on-call rotation for
it, and mentored two junior engineers on the team. That reads to me as
senior-level scope. Can the leveling committee take a look at that before
finalizing? I'd rather get the level right now than negotiate around it
later."

Outcome: recruiter takes the specifics back to the panel. Committees can
and do revisit a leveling call when given concrete scope evidence, provided
it's raised before the offer is drafted — after the offer letter is signed,
the same request requires a much higher bar (usually a formal promotion
cycle) to revisit.
```

The lever here isn't aggression — it's giving the committee concrete, specific evidence to justify a level change, framed as a factual question rather than a demand.

slides.sectionTitle: Why level rarely moves after you start
slides.markdown:
Once you start, your level is locked into the company's HR system, tied to a specific pay grade, org chart position, and (at larger companies) a formal job architecture that other systems reference — performance calibration, headcount ratios, even legal pay-equity audits. Un-doing that requires a promotion, which is a separate, slower process gated by a review cycle, not a comp conversation.

This is the senior-level nuance new candidates often miss: negotiating the *level* is a narrow window that exists almost entirely between "verbal offer" and "signed offer letter." Once you accept, you've effectively converted a flexible pre-hire negotiation into a fixed internal data point that will take a full promotion cycle (often 12-24 months minimum) to change.

This is also why experienced negotiators treat the level conversation as strictly separate from, and prior to, the dollar-amount conversation — conceding on level to "keep things friendly" costs far more than conceding a few thousand dollars of base.

slides.sectionTitle: Negotiating within the band vs. negotiating the level
slides.markdown:
These are two different negotiations with different ceilings. Negotiating **within a band** (asking for a higher base, more equity, a signing bonus) is a routine conversation a recruiter can usually resolve alone, and typical movement is a single-digit percentage of the initial number. Negotiating the **level itself** changes which band you're negotiating within — and the ceiling on that conversation is an entirely different, usually much larger, number, because you're moving to a different band's floor and cap.

A practical rule: if your target number is inside the band one level up from what you were offered, that's a signal to negotiate level, not just base — pushing hard for a within-band number that already sits above the band's typical max just makes the recruiter's job of getting an exception approved harder, when a level conversation might get you there more directly. [Reading and evaluating a written offer](reading-evaluating-offer) covers how to convert a full offer into one comparable number before deciding which lever to pull.

slides.sectionTitle: What to lock down before you negotiate anything else
slides.markdown:
Before engaging with any specific number, confirm three things: the exact level title and internal band (ask the recruiter directly — this is a normal question), whether that band is location-adjusted (a senior band in a lower-cost-of-living office can pay meaningfully less than the same title elsewhere), and whether the level was calibrated against your actual demonstrated scope or defaulted to a generic guess based on years of experience alone.

Getting these three answers first turns the rest of the negotiation from guesswork into arithmetic — you'll know whether you're negotiating for more room inside the right band, or whether the band itself is the thing to contest.
